verses.1: Al-Mizan takes tasāʾul to mean either people questioning one another or a group repeatedly questioning another person, so the hearers may have questioned each other or the Prophet. The warning tone identifies them as the Meccan polytheists who denied prophethood and the hereafter, not believers or a mixed audience. The rhetorical question censures their inquiry as absurd, since its answer is evident.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan identifies the “great news” as the Resurrection and afterlife: ʿaẓīm magnifies its importance, the subsequent proofs and description of Judgment confirm this, and it accords with the primary Meccan theme, especially of the early al-ʿatāʾiq chapters. It rejects taking the news simply as the Qurʾan’s content, though that is implied, because context does not support it. It also rejects making it every disputed religious subject—God, attributes, angels, messengers, Resurrection, Paradise, and Hell—because these are implications of Resurrection and would make the chapter’s account of Judgment secondary; moreover, the polytheists already admitted the Creator and angels.

Al-Mizan says the polytheists agreed in denying Resurrection but differed in their grounds: impossibility (34:7), remoteness (23:35-36), doubt (27:66), or obstinate defiance despite certainty (67:21). Warned of recompense, they were deeply affected and began asking about this unprecedented news, perhaps asking the Prophet and believers when the promise would be fulfilled (10:48, 21:38, 27:71, 34:29, 36:48, 67:25), and perhaps the People of the Book, especially Jews. The dialogue questions their questioning in (78:1), names its object in (77:2-3), and answers it with the threat in (77:4-5). Other exegetical constructions are set aside as out of keeping with the context.

verses.4: Al-Mizan reads kallā as a prohibitive “nay”: the polytheists must cease an inquiry born of their divided denial of the hereafter, for the news will soon disclose itself and they will know it. The wording is a threat, comparable to the warning in (26:227).
verses.5: Al-Mizan says the repeated “nay” reinforces both the prohibition and the threat of the preceding verse. Together (78:4-5) show that those questioning were deniers of Resurrection and requital, not believers or the whole society.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan reads (78:6-16) as proof that the great news—Resurrection and requital—will occur, so the deniers will soon witness it. The ordered, finely balanced world of earth, sky, night, day, and reproducing humanity cannot be futile; beyond its changing impermanence must be an enduring order in which righteousness and wrongdoing show their outcomes. Fiṭrah commands conscientiousness and forbids mischief, yet this world does not adequately display the Godwary’s felicity or the corrupting person’s wretchedness. It would be irrational for God to instil such moral inclinations without their reality or effect; recompense for good and evil therefore follows, as in (38:27-28).

The commentary distinguishes this argument, which proves Judgment’s necessary occurrence, from the sound but contextually weaker argument that the signs prove God’s power to restore a creation He first made: that proves only possibility. Mihād means a floor-covering, background, or settled place for human activity, so the earth is made a peaceful habitation. Awtād, thick nails or stakes, describes mountains apparently because volcanic eruptions leave solidified magma rooted toward the earth’s centre and stabilizing underlying agitation. The alternative that “stakes” means their life-sustaining resources departs from the apparent sense without need.

verses.8: Al-Mizan takes azwāj as male-and-female pairs, created for procreation and the continuance of humankind as God wills. It rejects readings of azwāj as similar forms, racial classes, or the sperm and ovum. The shift from third-person description to direct second-person address highlights the verse’s decisive, irrefutable proof.
verses.9: Al-Mizan defines subāt as rest and comfort: sleep suspends bodily faculties from daily activity so they recover from earned exhaustion. Qaṭʿ, severance from activity, is close to this meaning. It rejects interpreting subāt as death: (6:60) calls sleep tawaffī, taking in full, not mawt, and (39:42) explicitly distinguishes sleep from death.
verses.10: Al-Mizan says night conceals visible things in darkness like clothing covers a body, fitting God’s plan that people cease work, return to home and family, and rest. It rejects the suggestion that night is a removable garment laid over the day as inconsistent with the human benefit emphasized by the surrounding verses and with the next verse.
verses.11: Al-Mizan, citing al-Rāghib, distinguishes ʿaysh, animal life, from ḥayāh, which also applies to God and angels. Maʿāsh may grammatically be a verbal, temporal, or locative noun; here it most likely makes daytime the time or place for living and seeking provision from the Lord. The alternative verbal-noun reading, with an omitted annexed noun, means making the day for seeking one’s livelihood and effectively reaches the same sense.
verses.12: Al-Mizan describes the seven heavens as firmly and solidly built above humankind.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains wahhāj as intensely hot and bright, and identifies the radiant lamp as the sun.
verses.14: Al-Mizan glosses thajjāj as pouring, abundant water and al-muʿṣirāt as rainclouds, while reporting the alternative that they are winds which condense clouds into rain. The rain brings forth the grains and plants that feed people and other animals, and luxuriant alfāfan gardens: gardens of intertwined trees. Some say alfāf is a plural without a singular.

verses.17:
Al-Mizan calls the Day of Judgment al-faṣl because God’s judgment separates people and gives each what their deeds deserve. Mīqāt is its fixed deadline, the final appointment for judgment among them. Inna and the past-tense kāna stress the Day’s certainty in God’s primordial knowledge: when He created the heavens and earth and ordered the universe, He eternally knew that the world would remain incomplete without this end at which disputes are settled.

The Trumpet gathers people in swiftly moving afwāj, apparently as in (17:71). Heaven is opened and becomes gates connecting the human and angelic worlds; Al-Mizan rejects both an omitted “possessing” and merely emergent paths as unwarranted impositions. Mountains moved and demolished lose their form and become sarāb, not literally pools of reflected water but an empty appearance without the reality of mountains. This accords with the Hour’s quake (22:1), their movement, leveling, running-sand, carded-wool, pulverization, and scattering in (52:10), (69:14), (73:14), (101:5), (56:5), and (77:10). It compares their obliteration with nations made folktales in (34:19) and (23:44), and false gods reduced to names in (53:23), and relates the image to (27:88) if that verse also concerns the Hour’s quake.

verses.21: Al-Mizan, following al-Mufradāt, explains raṣad as watchful guarding and mirṣād as a place deliberately set for watching, so Hell lies in ambush for those who pass over it, as (19:71) says. It compares marṣad in (9:5). Maʾāb, derived from return, makes Hell the transgressors’ final resort: by exceeding the limits through ṭughyān, they have made it their destination and return to it when life ends.

verses.23:
Al-Mizan defines aḥqāb as successive, unspecified long periods and understands the transgressors as deliberate, hostile disbelievers, as (78:27-28) confirms. “Age after age” can therefore mean unending residence and does not contradict verses affirming the disbelievers’ eternal stay. It reports a plausible alternative, provided context permits it: the denial of coolness and drink in (78:24-25) applies to one succession of ages, followed forever by other conditions. Proposed singulars include ḥuqb, ḥuqub, ḥaqb, and ḥiqbah; al-Rāghib calls ḥiqbah an unspecified span. Reports fixing a ḥuqb at forty, eighty or eighty-odd, or 70,000 years—and even a 360-day year of thousand-year days—have no Qurʾanic or lexicographical evidence.

The contrast of coolness and drink means no cooling relief, such as shade, and no drink; dhawq thus covers any enjoyment or access. Ḥamīm is scalding water and ghassāq the pus exuded by Hell’s dwellers. Wifāq establishes exact correspondence between recompense and voluntary action: because an act is done for its result, giving the result is in a sense giving the action itself, as (66:7) states. The grammatical possibilities for wifāq—an active-participial use, an omitted “possessing,” or emphatic use of the verbal noun—each preserve that fitting proportionality.

verses.27: Al-Mizan says kidhdhāban intensifies surprise at the deniers’ persistence. Their fitting punishment follows because they expected no reckoning, hoped for no coming life, denied the signs proving it, rejected monotheism and prophethood, and exceeded the limits of servitude. Having disregarded God, they are deprived of eternal bliss and meet only wretchedness and torment, as the next warning in (78:30) declares.

verses.29: Al-Mizan gives two readings of kitāban: a sublime book in which everything, including deeds, is clearly recorded, comparable to (36:12), or a circumstantial qualifier meaning everything was recorded while written, whether in the Preserved Tablet or individual records of deeds. Because iḥṣāʾ and kitābah both preserve by recording, each may be read through the other: recording everything with a complete record, or writing everything with a complete writing. Either way, the verse completes the preceding justification: their requital accords with their deeds because God has recorded all of them.
verses.30: Al-Mizan takes the opening faʾ as the conclusion of the preceding account of punishment and as a declaration that the condemned have no hope of deliverance or comfort. The shift from third person to direct address treats them as present for reprimand. Each punishment is followed by another, accumulating forever; the verse therefore explains “abiding therein for ages” in (78:23) as unending punishment without termination.
verses.31: Al-Mizan, citing al-Rāghib, defines fawz as attaining good in security: deliverance from evil and attainment of good. An editorial note distinguishes it from falāḥ, which stresses immunity from pain, while fawz stresses enjoyment. Mafāz may be either the verbal noun “triumph” or the place of triumph. The Godwary’s triumph consists of enclosed orchards (ḥadāʾiq), vineyards and grapes (aʿnāb), kawāʿib—young maidens whose breasts have begun to round—of equal age (atrāb), and dihāq cups brimming with drink.

verses.35:
Al-Mizan says Paradise contains neither futile speech nor mutual denial, so its speech is true and effective. An editorial note records that kidhdhāb may instead be the intensive form of kadhib, yielding no vain, much less false, speech. The Godwary receive this as jazāʾ from the Prophet’s Lord: the possessive both honors the Prophet and accords with the Qurʾan’s avoidance of ascribing the transgressors’ requital to God, since they caused their own fate (3:182, 8:51).

Al-Mizan records three grammatical accounts of ʿaṭāʾan ḥisāban: it may be a circumstantial qualifier for jazāʾan, a specification, or an emphatic absolute object, in each case expressing a reward from the Lord as a reckoned bounty. An authorial note treats ḥisāb as a verbal noun functioning as a passive participle, “measured, calculated, proportionate”; an editorial note also allows “sufficient, ample.” The recurrence of ḥisāb after the transgressors’ retribution and the Godwary’s reward confirms the reckoning central to the Day of Judgment (78:17).

verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains “your Lord” as the Lord of heavens, earth, and all between them: the Prophet’s Lord governs everything, unlike the polytheists’ division of lordship among beings, with God as lord of lords or heaven alone. An editorial note observes that this formulation is almost a verbatim translation of the Shema in Deuteronomy 6:4. Al-Raḥmān, an intensive derivative of raḥmah, means that His universal lordship embraces all in mercy; only those insufficient through their own wrong choice deprive themselves of it. The transgressors’ opting out of servitude is therefore supreme wretchedness.

“Whom they will not be able to address” means that creatures cannot call God to account—asking why He did or omitted something—as (21:23) states. In its context, and particularly (78:38), it concerns Judgment: no one may contest how He recompenses servants, intercede, or seek equivalent relief. Angels likewise do not object, for they act only by His command (21:26-27), and the Spirit does not oppose the truth, being God’s word (16:40), while God is Manifest Truth (24:25). “Address” thus covers intercession, ransom, bargaining, friendship, supplication, and petition, as (2:254), (2:123), and (11:105) show.

The pronoun includes all who are gathered—Spirit, angels, humans, and jinn—befitting the manifestation of divine grandeur. Al-Mizan finds unlikely that it means transgressors, given their remoteness in the context, or the Spirit and angels, since neither had been mentioned; both alternatives also miss that the address at issue is intercession and similar deliverance.
verses.38: Al-Mizan takes yawm as the temporal qualifier of “they will not be able to address” in (78:37), rather than of “they will not speak,” because a temporal qualifier normally attaches to the preceding event. An editorial note says this syntactic choice partly grounds the reading; without it, the alternative is quite apparent and plausible. The unqualified Spirit is the being of divine command in (17:85), not the higher angelic orders, their guards, or an angel governing them, for which no evidence exists. Gabriel, human spirits awaiting return to their bodies between Trumpet blasts, and the Qurʾan’s manifested teachings and predictions can be called rūḥ in other verses—(26:193), (16:102), (19:17), (15:29, 38:72), and (42:52)—but there rūḥ is qualified or annexed; the last two readings also impose an unwarranted sense on this verse. Ṣaffan means standing while arraying, and the juxtaposition permits the inference that the Spirit forms one array and the angels another. The commentary makes “they will not speak” explain the preceding inability to address: the referent is all gathered beings—Spirit, angels, humans, and jinn—not only the Spirit and angels or people. None speaks unless the All-Merciful permits, as in (11:105), and ṣawāban means speech wholly free of falsehood and error. Permission therefore belongs only to speakers of truth, comparable to (43:86). Al-Mizan rejects the alternative that the exception concerns persons spoken for—approved monotheists who said lā ilāh illā Allāh, related to (21:28)—because the negation applies to all speech, so the exception must introduce permitted speakers, not permissible subjects. In its wider discussion, Al-Mizan says rūḥ first suggests life but is neither human nor animal only. The best definition is the unqualified Spirit “of the command of my Lord” (17:85). God’s command is the existentiating “Be” in (36:82-83): ījād and wujūd considered in relation to God, not apparent causes. That explains Jesus as God’s word and spirit in (4:171), conceived without ordinary means, like Adam’s creation in (3:59). Most references qualify spirit—human spirit from God in (15:29, 38:72) and (32:9), God’s Spirit in (19:17), a spirit from Him in (4:171), and the Holy Spirit in (2:87, 2:253)—but the unqualified Spirit in (97:4) and (70:4) apparently is an ethereal being distinct from angels. The Qurʾan describes three human levels: the spirit blown into all humans, where min indicates origin and nafh blowing; a believers’ spirit, where bi indicates causality and taʾyīd support (58:22); and the prophets’ higher, holy spirit, again by taʾyīd (2:87, 2:253). Qudus means holiness, purity, or immaculateness; an editorial note adds that “Holy Spirit” is customary but not linguistically exact, since qudus is not an adjective of rūḥ. From these and (97:4), Al-Mizan infers that qualified spirits stand to the unqualified Spirit as emanation to emanator or shadow to body, by God’s leave. An editorial note explains this as causal dependence without depletion and calls the absolute Spirit a transcendent, temporal creation of God, comparing the relation to atman and Atman. Spirits ascribed to angels are likewise emanations or diffusions of the Spirit. Angels are purely spiritual, though variously near or distant from God; any bodily appearance is tamaththul, as in (19:17), not bodily incarnation. Thus the Qurʾan calls them spirit rather than saying spirit is blown into them; nafh suits humans, compounded of lifeless body and living soul. Because life has degrees, spirit has degrees: believers’ spirit is higher and more effective than the universal one, as (6:122) depicts the believer’s light and the disbeliever’s death despite possessing ordinary human spirit. Al-Mizan also infers a degree in plants from the Qur’an’s repeated descriptions of earth’s revivification; the prophets’ supporting spirit is higher still. The Spirit of command in (40:15) and (42:52) may correspond to the believers’ spirit or the prophets’ Holy Spirit; God knows best. An editorial note directs to earlier discussions under (6:122) and (17:85).
verses.39: Al-Mizan says dhālika points back to the Day of Judgment, and its use for something distant underscores that Day’s immensity and magnificence. It is ḥaqq: certain and inevitable. The final command draws the chapter’s proofs and description to their conclusion: whoever wills should take a maʾāb, synonymous with marjaʿ, with the Lord—a return in which the Godwary obtain their reward and are secure from the transgressors’ punishment.
verses.40: Al-Mizan identifies the near punishment as hereafter punishment: what is inevitable is practically near, and the deeds for which one will be requited already adhere most closely to the person. A person will await the consequences of deeds sent ahead; alternatively, the deeds themselves will appear before their doer, as in (3:30). The Day’s intensity makes the faithless wish to be dust, for dust lacks intelligence and will and so is not subject to voluntary action or its consequences.
